title: Check: DaemonSets and StatefulSets
description: Five questions on the two controllers that are not Deployments.

options.text: A fixed number of Pods cluster-wide

questions.explanation: A DaemonSet places a copy on every node that matches its selector, and adds one automatically when a node joins - which is why log shippers and CNI agents use it.

questions.prompt: What does a StatefulSet give a Pod that a Deployment does not? Choose all that apply.

options.text: A stable, ordinal name such as web-0

questions.explanation: Stable identity and per-Pod storage are the whole point. Nothing about a StatefulSet makes scheduling faster.

questions.prompt: By default, how does a StatefulSet scale up?

options.text: In order, 0 then 1 then 2, waiting for each to be Ready

questions.explanation: Ordered, one at a time, each waiting for the previous to be Running and Ready. Scale-down runs in reverse. `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` opts out.

questions.prompt: A StatefulSet needs which kind of Service for stable DNS names?
questions.explanation: A headless Service gives each Pod its own DNS record - web-0.svc, web-1.svc - instead of load-balancing across them.

questions.prompt: You delete a StatefulSet. What happens to the PVCs it created?

options.text: They are kept, so the data survives
They are moved to the default namespace

questions.explanation: PVCs from volumeClaimTemplates outlive the StatefulSet on purpose - deleting data should never be a side effect. Remove them by hand when you mean it.
